clusters.label: Jevons paradox explained
clusters.description: General explainers and policy-oriented analyses of how efficiency gains can raise total resource consumption, with historical context and implications for sustainability and economic growth.

clusters.label: Rebound effect economics
clusters.description: Articles defining direct and indirect rebound effects and weighing the evidence on how much efficiency savings are eroded by behavior and economic responses.

clusters.label: Efficiency as climate strategy
clusters.description: Institutional reports from agencies and think tanks arguing efficiency is the fastest, cheapest route to decarbonization, alongside renewables and electrification.

clusters.label: Consumer efficiency basics
clusters.description: Introductory guides defining energy efficiency and offering practical advice, standards, and Energy Star-type tips for saving energy and money in homes and buildings.

clusters.label: Jevons and AI economics
clusters.description: Pieces prompted by DeepSeek arguing cheaper computing and AI will increase demand, drawing on historical technology examples to explain why efficiency spurs usage.

clusters.label: AI's environmental footprint
clusters.description: Critical takes questioning whether Jevons paradox applies to AI, examining data centers, hardware, energy and water use, and the polarized environmental debate.

propositions.statement: Efficiency gains can produce rebound effects that raise total resource consumption, so efficiency can increase rather than reduce overall use (the Jevons paradox).

stances.claim: Jevons Paradox holds that efficiency makes a resource cheaper and so raises its total consumption, as with British coal use tripling by 1900.
Increasing energy efficiency may drive growth in global energy consumption and emissions, contrary to common expectations.
Efficiency improvements can increase consumption through rebound effects because lower costs make resource use more attractive.
The Jevons paradox occurs only when a technology makes an existing process more efficient and demand is highly price-sensitive.
Jevons Paradox holds that efficiency gains lower the cost of a resource, which raises demand and can increase total consumption.
Jevons Paradox says efficiency gains reduce a resource's cost, making it more attractive and increasing demand and total consumption.
Efficiency gains tend to increase collective resource consumption because they cheapen services, so people use more of them.
In The Coal Question (1865), Jevons argued that increased energy production efficiency leads to more consumption, a view now known as the Jevons paradox.
When a resource becomes more efficient to use, total consumption often rises rather than falls, as in coal engines, cars and AI.
Jevons paradox operates globally: since 1990 energy efficiency rose 36% while total energy consumption rose 63%.
For the end uses with available US studies, estimates of the rebound effect range from very low to moderate.
Jevons argued that improved efficiency lowers costs and prices, which drives higher demand and increases total consumption.
Jevons' paradox is far from a deterministic law, and market saturation and capital limits can dampen or eliminate the rebound effect in high-tech sectors.
Amory Lovins argues David Owen's rebound claims about energy efficiency are counterfactual, discredited, and were rebutted by several experts.
Jevons Paradox holds that efficiency gains lower resource costs and can raise total consumption, as Jevons saw with coal and steam engines.
Jevons Paradox says efficiency improvements lower costs and stimulate demand, which can increase total resource consumption instead of conserving it.
The Jevons Paradox says efficiency gains can paradoxically increase total resource consumption, as with coal use after more efficient steam engines.
The Jevons Paradox says energy efficiency improvements can increase rather than decrease energy consumption.

propositions.statement: Jevons paradox applies to AI efficiency gains such as DeepSeek, so more efficient AI will increase total use of chips, data centers and energy.

stances.claim: Piao argues efficiency unlocks new demand, so cheaper AI will drive GPU sales and energy use.
Jevons' Paradox likely applies to DeepSeek's efficiency gains, so greater AI efficiency will drive greater use and keep GPUs and data centers critically important.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella invoked Jevons paradox to argue that more efficient AI, as shown by DeepSeek, will see its use skyrocket.
Efficiency gains in AI may not guarantee exponential demand for chips, GPUs and data centers.
Jevons' Paradox applies to AI: efficiency gains may spur increased overall consumption, producing rebound effects that offset the environmental benefits of efficiency.

propositions.statement: Efficiency alone is insufficient for sustainability and must be complemented by policies or behavioral measures addressing rebound.

stances.claim: Research shows 30 percent of the potential energy savings of efficient technologies is lost to social, cultural and economic factors, so human behavior must be addressed.
Relying solely on efficiency is insufficient for environmental goals and must be complemented by measures addressing rebound.
Sustainability cannot be achieved by technological innovation alone and requires continuous institutional and behavioral adjustment.
Policymakers should account for potential offsetting increases in consumption when developing resource management strategies.
Without conscious intervention efficiency leads to more consumption, so the key question is how to make efficiency actually reduce consumption.
Technology alone cannot solve resource scarcity and ecological damage without mindful policies and interventions.
Technology alone cannot guarantee absolute reductions in resource use; human behavior and markets shape outcomes.
Efficiency alone may not reduce total resource consumption, so policies such as carbon taxes or caps may be needed.
Efficiency alone is not a silver bullet for sustainability and could even worsen the problems it targets.
Pairing efficiency gains with policies that raise cost of use, such as cap and trade or green taxes, can control the rebound.
Technical efficiency alone cannot ensure net reductions in AI's environmental harm; its impact also depends on business incentives, market logics, governance, policymaking and social norms.

propositions.statement: The magnitude of the rebound effect is contested and difficult to measure.

stances.claim: The total magnitude of rebound or backfire is contentious and nearly impossible to calculate because efficiency effects propagate through the whole global economy.
The rebound effect is real, but its magnitude is debated, ranging from super conservation to backfire.
Understanding the Jevons Paradox requires complexity science, not reductionism, because a system changes its identity in response to innovation, which makes the rebound effect hard to quantify.
Economists agree the rebound effect exists but disagree about its magnitude and importance in real-world situations.
Economy-wide rebound effects may erode more than half of the expected energy savings from improved energy efficiency.
Rebound effects come in direct, indirect and economy-wide forms, and the economy-wide effect is the hardest to measure.
Economists debate the size of the rebound effect and the paradox's relevance to energy conservation.

propositions.statement: LED and other lighting efficiency gains have led to more lighting use that erodes the energy savings.

stances.claim: Examples include vehicle miles, LED lighting and data centres, where overall consumption has not fallen despite efficiency gains.
Cars and lighting show the paradox, as efficiency gains encouraged more driving and wider lighting use.
LED lighting is an example where cheaper lighting leads people to light more spaces, eroding expected energy savings.
LED lighting illustrates the paradox: cheaper lighting can lead to more lights and longer use.
A study of 300 years of lighting use in Britain found people spend roughly the same share of GDP, about 0.72%, on lighting regardless of efficiency.

propositions.statement: Energy efficiency is among the cheapest, fastest and most cost-effective ways to cut emissions and energy costs.

stances.claim: Energy efficiency is the cheapest and often most immediate way to reduce fossil fuel use, while cutting emissions, energy imports and costs.
Energy efficiency is the quickest and most affordable way to decarbonize the economy, and the IEA says it can deliver a third of emission reductions needed for 2050 net zero.
Energy efficiency is one of the fastest, most cost-effective ways to save money, cut emissions, create jobs and meet growing energy demand.
Federal officials such as Steven Chu portray energy efficiency as a cost-free way to cut oil use, emissions and consumer spending without sacrifice.
Energy efficiency is crucial for the energy transition because it eases energy security concerns, cuts costs, improves competitiveness and reduces grid investment needs.
Energy efficiency makes climate action faster, cheaper and more equitable, since today's energy system wastes two-thirds of global energy production, costing about $4.5 trillion yearly.
Energy efficiency is among the easiest and most cost-effective ways to cut energy waste, bills and air pollution.
Energy efficiency is a win-win that reduces energy use, emissions and customer costs, despite sometimes higher upfront costs.
Efficient energy use is the most important and economical way to provide future energy services, and the US could run its economy on 40 percent less primary energy by 2050.
Energy efficiency is the 'first fuel' of clean energy transitions, offering quick, cost-effective CO2 mitigation, lower bills and better energy security.
Efficiency is often the cheapest and most effective way to meet energy service demand while reducing climate impact.

propositions.statement: Efficiency reduces energy demand, easing grid expansion needs and helping integrate renewables.

stances.claim: Reducing energy demand lessens the need to expand the grid and accelerates the switch to renewables.
Efficiency lowers electricity demand, reducing the need for new generation and transmission and hedging against fuel price volatility.
Rising demand from electrification, data centers and cooling means utilities must prioritize efficiency to avoid costly grid expansion.
Efficiency measures facilitate renewable deployment, so integrated strategies are the most effective approach.
Energy efficiency lowers household energy bills and reduces strain on the grid, helping prevent blackouts at peak times.

propositions.statement: Global energy efficiency progress is falling short of the pace needed for climate goals.

stances.claim: Leaders' thinking about energy efficiency is stuck in the fossil fuel era, which jeopardizes global climate goals.
The world is not yet on track for SDG 7.3, as energy intensity improved only 1.8 percent annually in 2010-2020.
Efficiency improvements fell to about 1 percent in 2024 instead of doubling to 4 percent as pledged at COP28.
Efficiency is the largest single measure for avoiding energy demand in the Net Zero Scenario, with global energy intensity falling about 4% per year this decade.

propositions.statement: Jevons argued in The Coal Question that coal's finiteness and rising demand would limit British prosperity.

stances.claim: Because of The Coal Question, Jevons is regarded as the first economist of standing to develop an ecological perspective on the economy.
Jevons argued in The Coal Question that Britain's global supremacy was transitory because its primary energy resource, coal, is finite.

propositions.statement: A Jevons-style demand increase may raise labor demand in some occupations rather than cause mass job loss from AI.

stances.claim: Efficiency gains from automation may not free up workers for more valuable work, since employers may cut pay, hiring or add low-value work instead.
Jevons paradox is also cited as a reason AI may create more jobs in some occupations rather than cause mass layoffs.
Coders, translators and radiologists may be occupations where AI productivity gains coincide with growing demand, whereas farming shows demand does not always explode.

propositions.statement: Efficiency measures delivered large energy and emissions savings historically and can cut future energy needs substantially.

stances.claim: Efficiency measures already saved about 15 percent of energy bills in 2022 and could cut global energy costs 20-25 percent by 2030.
Energy efficiency avoided more energy consumption in IEA member countries during 1974-2010 than any single fuel supplied.
Efficiency accounted for 82% of global carbon emissions reductions between 2010 and 2022 and met 67% of US energy demand growth since 1950.
